newsitem.title: UK: LME copper, zinc attain new peaks, aluminium slips.
newsitem.headline: LME copper, zinc attain new peaks, aluminium slips.

text.p: LME copper extended gains above $2,500 per tonne on Thursday as speculators buoyed the market, but players were uncertain whether the market had a firm short-term underpinning.
Zinc also carved out fresh highs, but aluminium crumbled on disappointed liquidation and fund selling.
Three month copper prices shot up to a fresh one-year peak of $2,530 in the morning, but drifted back as profits were taken and wary participants stood back.
In the last few minutes of the afternoon kerb, speculators came in to push the market back towards the highs. It ended $20 higher at $2,526, but some analysts were sceptical.
"There was a concerted effort by the speculative community to get a good close," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
"I'm friendly to the market, but the market is over-extended. I think we need to see a pullback to $2,480 first."
The 14-day RSI was at 80, the highest since May 1996 when prices were surging ahead of the Sumitomo scandal.

The spreads were jerky as borrowing sent the cash/threes backwardation flaring out to $100 in the morning then back towards Wednesday night's level of $80/$85. On the afternoon kerb the spread ballooned again, finishing the day at $100/$110.
Zinc also hit fresh highs, lifted by renewed confidence after stocks fell by 3,800 tonnes.
"That allayed fears that the stock drawdowns were slowing," Bahr said.
But the market was still on the lookout for rumoured substantial deliveries into the Singapore warehouse, analyst William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff said.
Prices topped out at $1,370, the strongest since early September 1992.
Selling, thought to be of Chinese origin, capped the market, which ended $14 stronger at $1,364.
Aluminium gave up an early defensive position above $1,650, sinking to a low of $1,631 on disappointed liquidation and fund selling.
Last kerb business was at $1,633, down $19.
"We need a shake-out to get rid of the weaker longs," said Bahr.
Gloomy talk coming out of the Alumitech conference in the U.S. about loss in market share for aluminium cans added to the negative sentiment.
Nickel bottomed out at $7,540 in the morning, but bounced to halt a two-day slide, finishing $80 firmer at $7,640.

Lead built on Wednesday's strong move, adding $7 to close at $644. The market was poised to challenge its long-term downtrend around $648, now that the summer battery replacement market was around the corner, analysts said.
Tin was dull, edging up $15 to $5,770, while alloy finished little changed at $1,495/500.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
